rows.question: What is the notice period before filing a cheque bounce complaint?
queries: What is the notice period before filing a cheque bounce complaint?
dishonour of cheque for insufficiency of funds notice period for payment demand
The Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 section 138 notice demanding payment
rows.answer:
The notice period for making a demand for payment before filing a complaint is fifteen days from the date of receipt of the notice, as stated in Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 [1]. The Supreme Court judgment in Kamlesh Kumar versus State of Bihar & Anr. notes that after sending the notice, 15 days' time is to be given to the noticee from the date of receipt of the notice to make payment [12].

Conditions and time limits:
- The cheque must be presented to the bank within a period of six months from the date on which it is drawn or within the period of its validity, whichever is earlier [1].
- The payee or holder in due course must make a demand for payment by giving a notice in writing to the drawer within thirty days of receiving information from the bank regarding the return of the cheque as unpaid [1].
- The drawer of the cheque must fail to make payment of the money to the payee or holder in due course within fifteen days of receiving the notice [1].

Related provisions:
- Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 covers the dishonour of a cheque for insufficiency, etc., of funds in the account and the punishment for the offence [1].

rows.question: What is presumed about consideration for a negotiable instrument?
queries: What is presumed about consideration for a negotiable instrument?
negotiable instrument presumption as to consideration holder in due course
Negotiable Instruments Act section 118 presumption as to consideration
Negotiable Instruments Act section 9 holder in due course
rows.answer:
Every negotiable instrument is presumed to be made or drawn for consideration, and when it has been accepted, indorsed, negotiated, or transferred, it is presumed to have been accepted, indorsed, negotiated, or transferred for consideration, according to Section 118 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 [1]. 

As discussed in the Supreme Court judgment *K.P.O. Moideenkutty Hajee versus Pappu Manjooran and Anr.*, Section 118 imposes a duty on the court to raise a presumption in favour of the plaintiff that the instrument was made for consideration, which shifts the burden of establishing that the promissory note is not supported by consideration to the defendant [11].

Related provisions:
- Section 43 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, which states that a negotiable instrument made, drawn, accepted, indorsed or transferred without consideration creates no obligation of payment between the parties to the transaction [4].

rows.question: When can a contract be avoided if consent was obtained by coercion or misrepresentation?
queries: When can a contract be avoided if consent was obtained by coercion or misrepresentation?
contract voidable on account of coercion fraud misrepresentation
Indian Contract Act section 19 voidability of agreements without free consent
Indian Contract Act section 15 coercion defined and section 18 misrepresentation defined
rows.answer:
A contract can be avoided when consent to the agreement is caused by coercion or misrepresentation, making it a contract voidable at the option of the party whose consent was so caused, as provided under Section 19 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 [1]. 

However, if consent was caused by misrepresentation or by fraudulent silence, the contract is not voidable if the party whose consent was so caused had the means of discovering the truth with ordinary diligence, according to the exception in Section 19 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 [1]. Additionally, a fraud or misrepresentation that did not cause the consent of the party on whom it was practised or to whom it was made does not render the contract voidable under the explanation to Section 19 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 [1].

Related provisions:
- Section 19A of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 provides for the power to set aside a contract induced by undue influence [4].

rows.question: Who is competent to enter into a contract?
queries: Who is competent to enter into a contract?
competency to contract age of majority soundness of mind disqualified by law
Indian Contract Act section 11
Indian Contract Act section 12 mental capacity soundness of mind for contract
topSources: The Indian Council of World Affairs Act, 2001 s1
rows.answer:
Every person is competent to contract who is of the age of majority according to the law to which he is subject, who is of sound mind, and who is not disqualified from contracting by any law to which he is subject, as stated in Section 11 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 [1][12].

Related provisions:
- Section 12 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, which explains that a person is of sound mind for making a contract if capable of understanding it and forming a rational judgment as to its effect upon their interests [2][13].
- Section 10 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, which states what agreements are contracts, requiring them to be made by the free consent of parties competent to contract, for lawful consideration and with a lawful object [6][12][13].

rows.question: What is the punishment for murder?
queries: What is the punishment for murder?
punishment for murder causing death culpable homicide
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita section 103 punishment for murder
topSources: The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 s531
rows.answer:
Whoever commits murder shall be punished with death or imprisonment for life, and shall also be liable to fine, under Section 103 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, which replaced Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 [1][9]. In the case of State through Superintendent of Police, CBI/SIT etc. versus Nalini and Ors. etc. etc., the Supreme Court excerpt quotes the punishment for murder as death or imprisonment for life, and liability to fine [11]. In the case of Bharatkumar Rameshchandra Barot versus State of Gujarat, the Supreme Court upheld the award of life imprisonment under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 [12].

Related provisions:
- Section 104 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, which covers punishment for murder by life-convict [2].
- Section 101 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, which defines murder and replaced Section 300 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 [4][10].
- Section 105 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, which covers punishment for culpable homicide not amounting to murder and replaced Section 304 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 [3][9].
- Section 109 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, which covers attempt to murder [6].

rows.question: What is the punishment for theft?
queries: What is the punishment for theft?
punishment for theft Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita section 303 theft punishment
topSources: The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 s2

rows.answer:
Whoever commits theft shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both, under Section 303 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (which replaced Section 379 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860) [1][8]. 

For a second or subsequent conviction under Section 303 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, the punishment is rigorous imprisonment for a term not less than one year and up to five years, along with a fine [1].

In cases of a first conviction where the value of the stolen property is less than five thousand rupees, upon the return or restoration of the property's value, the offender shall be punished with community service under Section 303 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 [1].

Related provisions:

- Section 306 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 covers theft by a clerk or servant of property in possession of a master, punishable with imprisonment up to seven years and fine [7].

rows.question: When can a person accused of a non-bailable offence be released on bail?
queries: When can a person accused of a non-bailable offence be released on bail?

topSources: The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 s480
The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 s482

rows.answer:
A person accused of a non-bailable offence may be released on bail when arrested or detained without warrant by an officer in charge of a police station or when appearing or brought before a Court other than the High Court or Court of Session, provided there are no reasonable grounds for believing the person has been guilty of an offence punishable with death or imprisonment for life, and the person is not barred as a previously convicted person under the specified conditions [1]. 

Section 480 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (which replaced Section 437 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973) also allows a court or officer to release the accused on bail at any stage of investigation, inquiry, or trial if it appears there are not reasonable grounds for believing the accused committed a non-bailable offence, but there are sufficient grounds for further inquiry [1].

- The court may direct that a person otherwise barred by clause (i) or clause (ii) be released on bail if such person is a child, a woman, sick, or infirm [1].

rows.question: How is a sale of immovable property defined and completed?
queries: How is a sale of immovable property defined and completed?
sale of immovable property definition transfer of ownership price paid
The Transfer of Property Act 1882 section 54 sale how made delivery of property
The Transfer of Property Act 1882 contract for sale tangible immovable property
topSources: The Transfer of Property Act, 1882 s54
The Transfer of Property Act, 1882 s58
The Transfer of Property Act, 1882 s55
The Transfer of Property Act, 1882 s69
rows.answer:
A sale of immovable property is defined as a transfer of ownership in exchange for a price paid or promised or part-paid and part-promised, under Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 [1].

The completion of a sale requires the transfer of all rights and interests in the property possessed by a person with their free consent to another person for a price called consideration, so that the title passes from the seller to the buyer, as discussed in the Supreme Court judgment Lucknow Nagar Nigam & Others versus Kohli Brothers Colour Lab. Pvt. Ltd. & Others [11].

For tangible immovable property valued at one hundred rupees and upwards, or for a reversion or other intangible thing, the transfer can be made only by a registered instrument under Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 [1]. (Note: In the State of Assam, such transfer must be made by an instrument registered in the State of Assam, notwithstanding anything contained in the Indian Registration Act, 1908, under Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 [1]).
